title: Make the framework describe itself accurately in the five places it doesn't

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited a2fc8e3 with bookkeeping 62b68a4, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

Every requirement met. The one I went at hardest was Req 5, because it promotes a claim I flagged twice and carried as an open item — and the evidence for it turned out to be real and recorded.

================================================================
REQ 5 — MY OWN CARRIED ITEM, AND IT CLOSES FOR npm
================================================================

I raised this in sprint 17 ("does `Bash(npm publish *)` match a bare `npm publish`?"), carried it through sprint 18, where the comment correctly said "Confirmed: git. Inferred, not established: npm." Sprint 20 promotes npm. That is exactly the shape of the error this epic keeps making, so I went looking for the evidence rather than reading the citation.

It exists, and it is recorded in sprint 18's own LiveQA verdict:
    claude -p --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Bash(npm pack *)"
    task: run exactly `npm pack`, nothing appended, no arguments, no redirect
    RESULT: permission_denials 0, and bare-verb-probe-1.0.0.tgz was produced
And LiveQA's own reasoning about it is the part that makes it evidence rather than an absence: "The tarball is the part that matters: it proves the bare command actually RAN, rather than merely not being denied."

That answers sprint 18's own explicit warning — its file says "Zero denials get read as a working bound" was a named risk, and LiveQA had previously refused to score zero denials as evidence for exactly that reason. This probe does not rest on zero denials; it produces a positive artifact proving execution. Correct method, correctly reasoned, and it closes the question for npm.

The promotion is also correctly bounded, which the criterion asks about specifically: "Confirmed: git and npm. Inferred, not established: every other entry on this list -- promoting these two is not license to claim the general property." Exactly one entry promoted, general caveat intact. My carried item narrows to "every entry other than git and npm remains inferred" and stays on the list in that form.

================================================================
REQ 4 — MET, AND IT IS THE BEST THING IN THIS SPRINT
================================================================

The criterion says a method without its failure history reads as obvious and gets skipped. The paragraph names both prior wrong conclusions by sprint number (17 and 19), explains the mechanism of the error rather than just the fact of it — the role refused on its own judgement before the permission layer was ever consulted, and an honest reasoned refusal looks identical to an unobservable bound from outside — credits both reports as honest about what they found, gives the working method, and closes with "a method stated without this history reads as obviously correct and gets skipped by whoever tries it next."

That last clause is the criterion's own test, answered in the artifact. This is the second time this project has written down not just a correction but why the wrong version was believable, and it is the more useful half.

(My first grep missed the sprint numbers because they sit mid-paragraph rather than at line start. My tooling, not an omission — recording that because I nearly reported Req 4 as half-met on the strength of a bad grep.)

================================================================
REQS 1, 2, 3 — MET
================================================================

Req 1 — read cold against the standard that matters. LiveQA is now defined by function: "verify the released artifact in a real environment, after distribution — not a diff, not a promise, the actual thing." A project with no deployed product knows what to do: install the published package fresh into a scratch directory. The refusals the criterion names are intact and not softened — "You do NOT trust QA1's static pass, or anyone's 'it works.' You re-verify live, every time," and "you don't speculate, you don't theorize about the code." The browser is now the common case rather than the definition, in both the persona and the role table.

Req 2 — the contradiction is gone. The old text claimed LiveQA's gate did not apply to this repository. The new text states what the code actually does: cmd_complete refuses to close any sprint without a recorded LiveQA PASS, with no override. I checked the code rather than the claim — the enforcement is at sprint_lifecycle.py:1356, `if state["groundtruth_result"] != "PASS"`. (The sprint file cites :688, which is where it lived when the requirement was written; the line has moved, the enforcement has not.) Grepped the whole of CLAUDE.md for any remaining "does not apply" or skippable-gate language: none.
Worth recording what this unblocks: every sprint file since sprint 3 has carried a "LiveQA's gate is REDEFINED, not skipped" header specifically because CLAUDE.md said the opposite. That workaround is now unnecessary — which is what the Req 1 criterion is pointing at when it says the fourteen header paragraphs become unnecessary.

Req 3 — read as a consumer inside an installed target, which is the criterion's instruction. It cannot be read as licensing edits to their own scripts: "If you did not clone `fully-completely` itself to work on the framework — if you ran `npx fully-completely` or an equivalent installer into your own project — this whole section is not about you or your `scripts/`," and it redirects them to the section that does apply. It also names the near-miss rather than fixing it silently.
Verified in the actual installed artifact rather than in the source, since that is where the misreading happened: installed a fresh copy from this build into a scratch directory and confirmed the disambiguating clause is present in the target's own CLAUDE.md. The correction reaches the reader who needed it.

REQS 6, 7 — package.json 0.1.21, one line. No test files touched, which is correct for a prose-only sprint and is what Req 7 asked for rather than a gap. Ran everything: 171 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; ALL WORKTREE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.21 (first install)".

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. Now that Req 2 removes the contradiction, the "LiveQA's gate is REDEFINED, not skipped" header on
   every in-flight sprint file is redundant. Not this sprint's to remove and not a defect — but the
   next sprint file written should probably not carry it, and Master Controller may want to say so
   once rather than have it copied forward out of habit.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred (narrowed this
   sprint, not closed); the CLI-version-drift item, still the strongest-evidenced open item and still
   unscheduled; the empty-string ownedRepository declaration falling through silently; the --agents
   argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 20, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.21, then `verify-publish 20`.

Committing the build before the bookkeeping this time, deliberately, after last sprint's slip — noted and correct.

Worth saying once: this sprint corrected five self-descriptions, and three of them were things a downstream reader or a downstream team would have acted on. The one that nearly caused real damage — the own-tooling section read from inside an installed copy — is now verified fixed in the installed copy rather than in the source, which is the only place that check means anything.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.21 by upgrading a real 0.1.20 install in a scratch directory and reading the result from inside it. Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, 2026-09-05. No billed agent runs were needed — every criterion here is observable from the published artifact and a real upgrade.

ON REQ 1, IN PRACTICE — THE CRITERION ABOUT THIS DOCUMENT
The criterion asks me to write these notes without a redefinition paragraph and say whether one was needed. There is none above, and one was not needed.

Every previous report I have filed on this repository opened with some version of "no browser, the package is the product, per the sprint file's redefinition block" — because the gate was described by its usual surface, so any sprint without a web app had to argue its way back to being testable at all. That argument is now unnecessary: `liveqa.md` as shipped in 0.1.21 defines the work as verifying the released artifact in a real environment after distribution, and names `npx <package>@<version>` into a scratch directory as "the same gate as driving a browser, applied to a different kind of release, not a lesser substitute for one." Installing 0.1.21 and reading it is straightforwardly the gate. Nothing had to be redefined, so nothing was.

That is Req 1 working, and it is worth stating as an outcome rather than a formality: the redefinition paragraph was never information, it was fifteen sprints of re-deriving the same conclusion because the definition pointed at the wrong thing.

PROVENANCE
0.1.21 on the registry; gitHead f534e493084e301db4e7a403a7887d736d015e28 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events; QA1 PASS round 1. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 57 published files byte-identical to `git show f534e49:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum. Own registry query run before reading verify-publish's record.

"NO BEHAVIOR CHANGE" — VERIFIED, NOT ACCEPTED
The handoff describes this as pure documentation with no behavior change. That is exactly the claim a documentation sprint should be checked on, so I diffed the executable surface between published 0.1.20 and 0.1.21:
  scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py    SAME        scripts/install.js             SAME
  scripts/run-lifecycle.js       SAME        scripts/launcher/prompts.js    SAME
  scripts/launcher/agents.js     SAME        scripts/launcher/run-role.js   CHANGED
and for the one that changed, stripping comment lines from both versions leaves the code byte-identical. So the only executable file touched differs solely in comments, which is what Req 5 (a comment correction) predicts. The claim holds.

`node scripts/launcher_test.js` against the published package: ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED, 171 OK lines, exit 0. Req 7 asked to confirm the suites pass untouched rather than add tests for prose; they do. (My first attempt ran it inside the installed target and got a usage message — `launcher_test.js` is framework-only and is not shipped into a target install. Recorded so the bare version string in that output is not mistaken for a failure.)

THE CORRECTIONS REACH AN EXISTING INSTALL
Installed published 0.1.20 into a scratch directory, left every user-owned file untouched, upgraded to 0.1.21:
  "Upgraded 0.1.20 -> 0.1.21", exit 0, ZERO conflicts, 7 user-owned files replaced
  liveqa.md  555b9b41d321 -> 1e261d0e4d54
  CLAUDE.md  0fb16757aac8 -> 8bbdcfeae5ce
Both changed. This is the manifest mechanism doing the job sprint 6 built it for: before 0.1.6 none of these corrections would have reached anyone who had already installed, and every one of them is a correction to a document whose entire purpose is to be read by people who installed months ago.

Each correction, confirmed in the upgraded target rather than in the source repo:

Req 1 — `liveqa.md` now defines the gate by what it does. The `npx`-into-scratch route is named as the same gate, in the toolset section, with "not a lesser substitute for one" stated explicitly. Absent at 0.1.20 (0 occurrences of `npx`), present at 0.1.21 (3).

Req 2 — `CLAUDE.md`'s claim that LiveQA's gate does not apply here is gone: 1 occurrence at 0.1.20, 0 at 0.1.21. The replacement states the honest version — "LiveQA's gate applies here too, with a different surface, not a different rule" — and cites `cmd_complete` refusing to close any sprint without a recorded LiveQA PASS, with no override. It cites the function by name rather than by line number, which is the more durable form.

Req 4 — the forced-denial method is in `liveqa.md`, and it is better than the requirement asked for. My `"twice"` grep returned zero and I nearly recorded that as a gap; reading the actual passage, it names the two instances outright ("Sprints 17 and 19 both reported 'cannot be forced'") rather than counting them, explains why the failure mode looks identical to a sound bound from outside, and is explicit that neither report was wrong to record what it found. It then adds a safeguard nobody specified: "If you ever report a bound as unforceable, say which of these two methods you used." That converts a method into a checkable claim, which is the thing that actually prevents the recurrence.

Req 5 — `run-role.js`'s matcher comment promotes npm and keeps the caveat, precisely: "Confirmed: git and npm. Inferred, not established: every other entry on this list -- promoting these two is not license to claim the general property." It also preserves the distinction that mattered in the evidence: the bare `npm pack` "produced the actual tarball -- proof the command ran, not merely proof it wasn't denied."

REQ 3 — READ FROM INSIDE THE INSTALLED TARGET, WHICH IS THE READING THAT NEARLY CAUSED THE INCIDENT
The criterion is specific that this must be read from an installed copy, not from this repository, so that is where I read it. The section now opens before any of its old content:

  "**'This repository' in this section means the `fully-completely` framework's own upstream source
  repository -- the one this framework itself is built and released from -- never a downstream project
  you have installed `fully-completely` into.**"

and continues with the disambiguation a consumer actually needs: that `scripts/`, `.claude/` and `templates/` name directories which exist in their project too because the install manifest put them there, that this section does not license editing them, and that if they ran `npx fully-completely` rather than cloning the framework, "this whole section is not about you or your `scripts/`". It names the near-miss directly — "A downstream team nearly made exactly this misreading, on day one, and stopped only because their own boundary held."

Read cold, from inside a target, with no knowledge of this framework's history, I do not think the dangerous reading survives. The requirement asked that the misreading become impossible rather than merely unlikely; the strongest thing I can say from a live read is that the first sentence of the section now answers the question the misreading depends on, before the reader reaches anything that could be misread. That is as close to impossible as prose gets, and it is a real improvement over "correct but dangerous when read from a target."

WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
Everything here I ran directly: the content comparison, the executable-surface diff, the real upgrade, the test suite, and every quoted line read out of the upgraded target rather than out of this repository. Pipeman's "no behavior change" description was checked rather than relayed. QA1's two non-blocking notes (a stale line-number citation and a now-redundant header) were passed to me as Master Controller's to act on; I have not scored them and note only that Req 2's replacement text cites `cmd_complete` by name, which is the fix the line-number note points at.

One correction to my own method is recorded above rather than omitted: the `"twice"` keyword search that nearly produced a false gap on Req 4.

RECOMMENDATION
Ship-ready. Five self-descriptions were wrong or dangerous, all five are corrected, and the corrections demonstrably reach an install that already existed — which for a sprint made entirely of documentation is the only thing that distinguishes it from a commit nobody will ever read.

Two of these corrections came from findings at my own gates (the forced-denial method, and promoting npm), and both are written up more carefully in the shipped text than in the reports they came from. Nothing carries forward as a defect.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 20.
